en: The Secret Key to the Commentary on the Meaning of the Contemplation Gate of Cintāmaṇicakra Bodhisattva:
The syllable *Oṃ*. The meaning of the flowing forth of all phenomena. Taking non-attainment as the skillful means.
Awakening is unattainable.
The syllable *vaṃ* signifies the transcendence of all phenomena.
The path of language is unattainable.
The syllable *ra* signifies that all phenomena are free from dust.
Even "realization" is unattainable.
The syllable *Na* signifies the meaning of the gift of all dharmas.
Ultimately unattainable.
The syllable BA:
the ultimate meaning of all phenomena.
The nature and characteristics are unattainable. *Namaḥ*.
All phenomena are free from the grasping of a self and are unattainable.
The syllable HŪṂ.
Furthermore, the definitive meaning of all phenomena is likewise unattainable.
To the right, the aforementioned syllables are arranged in this manner.
All become the color of saffron.
They are drawn in from the mouth of the Honored One into the wheels of body, speech, and mind;
having been clearly arrayed therein, [they remain].
Examine each one with diligent and careful observation;
from this samaya, you shall swiftly attain all-knowledge.
Now, when the recitation count of the yoga method has been completed:
Then, one arranges the various syllables.
Furthermore, one arrays the *hrdaya-mantra* upon the body.
Then, one clearly contemplates and visualizes [the deities] above the syllables.
Like the sun first rising,
its radiance is brilliant and vast, reaching to the infinite limits;
such is this contemplative illumination.
Before long, one shall realize the samādhi of the dharmakāya.
Place the syllable Oṃ at the crown of the head; place the syllable Ra on the forehead;
distribute the syllable Ra over the two eyes; and contemplate the syllable Na at the mouth.
Place the syllable *pa* at the heart; place the two-syllable *namaḥ* on the two shoulders.
With the gateway of the syllable *pra*, one will swiftly awaken to the principle of non-arising and before long achieve accomplishment, attaining the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The Heart Mantra of Cintāmaṇicakra.
The arrangement of the Sanskrit syllables upon the moon disc of the bodhicitta.
The commentary on the meaning of the Cintāmaṇicakra mantra.

*Namo* (Na-mo): the meaning of taking refuge. *Ratnatrayāya* (Ra-ta-na-tra-ya-ya): the meaning of the Three Jewels; that is to say, taking refuge in and revering the Three Jewels. *Namo* (Na-mo): the meaning of bowing one’s head. *Āryāvalokiteśvarāya* (A-rya-va-lo-ki-te-shva-ra-ya): the Noble Avalokiteśvara. *Bodhisattvāya* (Bo-dhi-sat-tva-ya): the Bodhisattva. *Mahāsattvāya* (Ma-hā-sat-tva-ya): the Great Bodhisattva. *Mahākāruṇikāya* (Ma-hā-kā-ru-ni-kā-ya): the One of Great Compassion. *Tadyathā* (Ta-dya-tha): that is to say, opening the Tathāgatagarbha to explain the mantra. *Oṃ*: this syllable signifies the accomplishment of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The single syllable *Oṃ* consists of the three syllables *Oṃ*, *A-ma*, and *Ā*.
The syllable *Oṃ* signifies that the arising of all phenomena is unapprehendable.
The syllable *A* signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
The syllable *Ma* signifies that the self of all phenomena is non-apprehendible.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
The syllable Oṃ signifies the Nirmāṇakāya;
the syllable A signifies the Saṃbhogakāya;
the syllable Ma signifies the Dharmakāya.
By means of these three syllables, which accord with the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
one performs a prostration to all Tathāgatas;
this is also the meaning of "the crown of the Tathāgata’s unobservable head."

*Chakra* (the syllable *chak*) means "to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma" and also "to destroy. *Vartani* (the syllables *va*, *rt*, *a*, *ni*) means "to contemplate. *Tamaṇi* (the syllables *ta*, *ma*, *ṇi*) means "to think."
It is also the meaning of the Tathāgata-jewel.
There are six kinds of jewels because they can fulfill the wishes of sentient beings.
*Mahāpadma* (摩訶鉢那麼): the Great Lotus, which symbolizes the purification of all non-Dharmic defilements, for it is fundamentally unstained; *ru ru ru*.
This refers to the meaning of being free from dust and defilement.
Since there are two kinds of dust,
the term is repeated.
The two types of objects are the internal objects and the external objects.
The internal objects are the five sense faculties.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
and the external objects— visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—
constitute these two kinds of objects.
Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one accomplishes the wisdom of yogic contemplation.
*Tiṣṭha*. (Tiṣṭha) [Sanskrit: tiṣṭha].
The commentary states that this refers to the meaning of "abiding," and it is also called the meaning of "non-abiding.
Non-abiding serves as the foundation for all phenomena.
It is also called "non-abiding nirvana," because it does not abide in saṃsāra.
Due to great wisdom, one is not attached to saṃsāra;
due to great compassion, one does not abide in nirvana.
*Jvala*. The commentary explains this as having the meaning of "blazing.
Its light shines brilliantly, pervading the ten directions, the void, and the *dharmadhātu*.
He awakens all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble assemblies,
who descend and gather from all directions;
he summons down all the classes of devas, nāgas, and the eightfold host, as well as all sentient beings.
By the power of bestowing benefit:
*akṣarya* (meaning "invocation"). *Ā-kṣa-rya*.
The meaning is "summoning."
By means of this invocation,
the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings shall arrive in response to the summons.
All clouds gather to bestow empowerment, protection, and mindfulness.
The syllable *HŪṂ* signifies that all phenomena are without cause;
it is also called the Bodhimanda.
As stated in the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-sūtra*,
as soon as one generates the bodhicitta, one immediately sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and turns the wheel of the true Dharma.
Through this correspondence,
this single syllable of the mantra is able to bring about the realization of all Buddha-dharmas;
at every moment of realizing the Buddha-dharmas, one attains awakening.
Possessing the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*),
he proceeds directly to the ultimate point and sits upon the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*).
When the four māras appear before him, he enters the samādhi of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-samādhi*).
By subduing the four māras, one attains perfect enlightenment.
The four māras are:
the māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra), the māra of afflictions (kleśamāra), the māra of death (mṛtyumāra), and the celestial māra (devaputramāra).
All are spontaneously subdued.
Furthermore, as for the statement that "dharmas have no cause," it means that all dharmas are without cause.
In accordance with ultimate truth, there is also no attainment of a fruit;
because cause and effect do not exist, it is primordially pure.
The syllable *PHAṬ* signifies the meaning of destruction.
It is also said to have the meaning of "crushing and destroying.
When one attains Buddhahood, one crushes and destroys the four māras.
It is also said that among the three virtues (triguṇa), [it corresponds to the virtue of power].
The meaning is attained within the virtue of abandonment;
by means of wisdom,
one completely abandons the afflictions and habitual tendencies of the nine stages across the three realms.
Having fully perfected both types of provisions— merit and wisdom—
they regard all sentient beings from time immemorial as their own kin; thus,
out of mindfulness of their kindness, [they act].
He proceeded to the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned to proclaim the twelvefold wheel of Dharma.
The syllable *ṭha* signifies the meaning that all phenomena are unattainable.
The letter *Ṭha* in the Sanskrit script has the shape of a half-moon.
The commentary explains that it signifies that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*),
taking non-apprehension as the skillful means.
Since it accomplishes the emptiness of sentient beings (sattva-śūnyatā) as half [of the whole],
the meaning of "sarva" and so forth— which is beyond verbal expression—
constitutes the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
The meaning of the syllable *pūrṇa* is also called the meaning of the accomplishment of great merit.
The syllable *haḥ* signifies the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*).
May all sentient beings accumulate great merit and virtue, sever the afflictions, secondary afflictions, and all habitual tendencies,
and may the teaching of the pervasive syllable fill their own and others' bodies.
The practitioner of yoga who has realized the nirvana without remainder and without abiding should form the mudrā and recite the mantra,
fixing the mind with single-pointed concentration upon this single syllable.
By means of contemplation that accords with the principle of ultimate reality,
one is able at that time to eliminate [dualistic grasping] regarding the subject, object, self, and others, and through the great compassion that perceives them as equal and of one essence,
suddenly amasses all merit and wisdom.
Now, having dispelled all calamities and untimely deaths,
people of the world rejoice upon seeing and hearing this;
the words they utter are respected and followed by devas and humans, who dare not transgress them.
At the time of death, the assembly of sages will appear before them,
and they shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss within the Great Assembly.

Born by transformation from a lotus flower, one beholds Amitāyus Buddha and hears the True Dharma, thereby suddenly realizing unsurpassed bodhi. [This concludes] the verse on the six-armed form of Cintāmaṇicakra Bodhisattva.
Holding a wish-fulfilling jewel in his hand, with six arms and a golden body,
his crown adorned with jewels; the Sovereign King, whose first hand is in the gesture of preaching the Dharma,
contemplates out of compassion for sentient beings.
The second holds the jewel of intent, capable of fulfilling all wishes;
the third holds a rosary to deliver beings from the suffering of the animal realm.
With his left hand pressing down upon Mount Potalaka, he achieves unshakable stability.
The second hand holds a lotus, capable of purifying all that is contrary to the Dharma;
The third hand holds a wheel, capable of turning the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.
Because it is able to bestow [benefits] accordingly, the mountain symbolizes immovability.
Because the nature of the lotus is unstained, And because the wheel destroys obstacles and afflictions,
The six arms are extensively adorned; Able to traverse the six realms through the skillful means of great compassion,
They sever the suffering of all sentient beings.
From the body flow a thousand rays of light, Which, according to one's recollection, can universally illuminate;
Like a bright mirror, they are able to manifest myriad forms.
The self-mind is fundamentally unarisen, For the nature of phenomena is perfectly quiescent.
As stated in the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-sūtra*:
"The Heart-to-Heart Mantra (Cittacittamantra), the syllable Oṃ, signifies the meaning of the flowing forth of all dharmas."
Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means,
one awakens to the fact that nothing can be apprehended.
The syllable *vaḥ* signifies the transcendence of all phenomena.
The path of language is severed and unattainable.
The syllable *ra* signifies that all phenomena are free from dust;
even this realization is unattainable.
The syllable *na* signifies the meaning of the gift of all dharmas;
it is ultimately unattainable.
The syllable *pa* signifies the ultimate truth of all dharmas.
The nature and characteristics are unapprehendable.
In the syllable *namaḥ*, the meaning of the departure from the grasping at a self in all phenomena is unapprehendable.
In the syllable *hūṃ*, the definitive meaning of all phenomena is likewise unapprehendable.
As described above, arrange the various syllables.
Draw them in the color of saffron.
They shall be pure and adorned, forty-eight in number.
Revised by Zunjiao Xingji.
